lead: This unit turns probability from event counting into a tool for random variables. You learn to condition, reverse conditions with Bayes, describe variables by pmf, pdf and CDF, compute moments and MGFs, bound tail probabilities, and derive the distribution of a transformed variable. After it you can set up and solve semester-3 probability problems and carry the ideas into standard distributions, joint distributions and statistics.
about: This unit builds a working language for uncertainty. Chapter 2.1 sets sample spaces, events and the three axioms. Chapter 2.2 adds conditional probability and independence. Chapter 2.3 turns conditioning into total probability and Bayes' theorem. Chapter 2.4 defines random variables through pmf, pdf and CDF. Chapter 2.5 computes expectation, variance and moments. Chapter 2.6 packages moments in the moment generating function. Chapter 2.7 gives Chebyshev's inequality as a distribution-free bound. Chapter 2.8 derives the distribution of a function of one random variable. After it, a student can model an uncertain quantity, compute its summary numbers, reverse conditional probabilities and transform variables for later units on standard distributions, joint distributions, estimation and testing.

chapters.idea: Probability is a number from 0 to 1 assigned to events in a sample space, obeying three axioms.
chapters.depth: Define random experiment, outcome ω, sample space Ω, event A⊆Ω, sure and impossible events. Cover union, intersection, complement, difference, De Morgan's laws, mutually exclusive and exhaustive events. State axioms: P(Ω)=1, P(A)≥0, and for disjoint A₁,A₂,… P(A₁∪A₂∪…)=ΣP(Aᵢ). Derive P(∅)=0, P(Aᶜ)=1−P(A), addition rule P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B), and monotonicity. Use classical equally likely counting and relative frequency only to motivate probability; some syllabi call Ω the universal set and events subsets. Keep permutations and combinations to simple equally likely cases.

figure.aria: A Venn diagram with set A containing 2 and 4, set B containing 3, and the shared region containing 6.
figure.caption: Event A = {2,4,6} and event B = {3,6}; the shared outcome 6 is in both events.

chapters.example: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. A={2,4,6}, B={3,6}. Find P(A), P(B), P(A∩B), P(A∪B), P(Aᶜ). A∩B={6}; P(A)=1/2, P(B)=1/3, P(A∩B)=1/6, P(A∪B)=1/2+1/3−1/6=2/3, P(Aᶜ)=1/2.
chapters.trap: Adding P(A)+P(B) double-counts A∩B; events are sets, not outcomes; P(∅)=0 follows, not an axiom in the standard list.
chapters.prereq: Basic set notation and fractions; Unit 1 averages are context only.
chapters.leave: Named distributions and the binomial probability law belong to Unit 3; advanced combinatorics is not needed here.

chapters.idea: Conditional probability limits the sample space to B; independence means that limit changes nothing.
chapters.depth: Define P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) for P(B)>0. Give multiplication rule P(A∩B)=P(A|B)P(B)=P(B|A)P(A). Draw tree diagrams for two-stage experiments; teach sampling with and without replacement. Define independence P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B) and extend to pairwise and mutual independence for three events. Contrast independent with mutually exclusive. Mention conditional independence P(A∩B|C)=P(A|C)P(B|C) in one line. Avoid using Bayes here except as a forward pointer.

figure.aria: Tree of two draws without replacement from 4 red and 6 blue balls: first branch blue has 6/10, then red has 4/9; the highlighted path is blue then red.
figure.caption: The highlighted path gives P(first blue and second red) = (6/10)(4/9) = 4/15.

chapters.example: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. Draw two balls without replacement. Find P(first blue), P(second red | first blue), P(first blue and second red), and P(second red). Are first blue and second red independent? P(first blue)=6/10=3/5; P(second red | first blue)=4/9; P(first blue and second red)=(6/10)(4/9)=4/15; P(second red)=2/5. They are not independent because 4/9 ≠ 2/5.
chapters.trap: P(A|B) is not P(B|A); independence is not the same as mutual exclusivity; without replacement changes the denominator.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 events, complements and the addition rule.
chapters.leave: Total probability and Bayes' theorem to 2.3; joint distributions and covariance to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A partition turns an event into weighted cases; Bayes' theorem reverses the condition.
chapters.depth: Define partition A₁,…,Aₙ: disjoint and union Ω. State total probability P(B)=ΣP(B|Aᵢ)P(Aᵢ). State Bayes' theorem P(Aⱼ|B)=P(B|Aⱼ)P(Aⱼ)/P(B) and name prior, likelihood, posterior, evidence. Use a tree or two-way table. Include a base-rate example. Some syllabi spell it Baye's theorem; use standard Bayes. Keep the denominator as total probability.

figure.title: Defect probability
figure.aria: Block diagram: machine M1 makes 60% at 2% defect and contributes 0.012; M2 makes 40% at 5% and contributes 0.020; the two contributions add to 0.032.
figure.caption: Total probability adds the defect contributions from the two machines: 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032.

chapters.example: Machine M1 makes 60% of items and M2 makes 40%. Defect rates are 2% for M1 and 5% for M2. An item is chosen at random. Find P(defective). If it is defective, find P(M1|defective). P(D)=0.6×0.02+0.4×0.05=0.032. P(M1|D)=0.012/0.032=0.375.
chapters.trap: Dividing by P(B) is compulsory; P(A|B) and P(B|A) are different; the partition must cover Ω without overlap.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 conditional probability and multiplication rule.
chapters.leave: Bayesian decision theory and classifiers to later courses; joint conditional distributions to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A random variable maps outcomes to real numbers, and its pmf, pdf or CDF gives the probability of each value or interval.
chapters.depth: Define random variable X:Ω→ℝ; discrete and continuous types. For discrete X, pmf p(x)=P(X=x), p(x)≥0, Σp(x)=1. For continuous X, pdf f(x)≥0, ∫f(x)dx=1, P(a<X≤b)=∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx, and P(X=x)=0. Define CDF F(x)=P(X≤x) for both types; list F nondecreasing, right-continuous, limits 0 and 1. For continuous, f(x)=F′(x) where differentiable. Show discrete CDF as a step function. Mention support. Some syllabi say distribution function for CDF and probability density for pdf.

figure.aria: Plot from x = 0 to 1 of the density f(x) = 2x and the CDF F(x) = x²; the area under f up to 0.6 is 0.36.
figure.caption: For f(x)=2x on (0,1), F(x)=x², so P(0.2<X≤0.6)=0.36−0.04=0.32.

chapters.example: A continuous random variable X has pdf f(x)=2x for 0≤x≤1, and f(x)=0 otherwise. Find the CDF F(x) and P(0.2<X≤0.6). F(x)=0 for x<0, F(x)=x² for 0≤x≤1, F(x)=1 for x>1; P(0.2<X≤0.6)=0.6²−0.2²=0.32.
chapters.trap: A pdf value is not a probability and may exceed 1; for continuous X use intervals, not points; the CDF uses ≤.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 axioms and Chapter 2.2 conditional probability for later distribution work; basic integration.
chapters.leave: Binomial, Poisson, normal and other named distributions to Unit 3; joint distributions to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Expectation is the long-run weighted average; variance measures spread around it; moments record shape.
chapters.depth: Define E[X]=Σx p(x) for discrete and ∫x f(x)dx for continuous, with absolute convergence. State E[g(X)]=Σg(x)p(x) or ∫g(x)f(x)dx. Cover linearity E[aX+b]=aE[X]+b. Define μ=E[X], Var(X)=E[(X−μ)²]=E[X²]−μ², SD σ=√Var(X). State Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X). Define raw moments μ′ᵣ=E[Xʳ] and central moments μᵣ=E[(X−μ)ʳ]. Link mean to first raw moment and variance to second central moment. Mention skewness and kurtosis as standardized third and fourth moments only in one line; their descriptive detail is Unit 1.

figure.title: Moments for two coin tosses
figure.aria: Table lists x=0,1,2 with probabilities 1/4,1/2,1/4 and weighted products; row sums give E[X]=1 and E[X²]=1.5.
figure.caption: Summing the third row gives E[X]=1; summing the fourth row gives E[X²]=1.5 and Var(X)=0.5.

chapters.example: X is the number of heads in two fair coin tosses. Find E[X], E[X²] and Var(X). P(X=0)=1/4, P(X=1)=1/2, P(X=2)=1/4. E[X]=0×1/4+1×1/2+2×1/4=1. E[X²]=0×1/4+1×1/2+4×1/4=1.5. Var(X)=1.5−1²=0.5.
chapters.trap: E[X²] is not (E[X])²; Var is not E[X²]; probabilities must sum to 1 before using the formula.
chapters.leave: MGFs to 2.6; skewness and kurtosis formulas and interpretation to Unit 1; named distribution moments to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: The MGF M_X(t)=E[e^{tX}] stores all moments as coefficients of its power series, so derivatives at 0 give moments.
chapters.depth: Define M_X(t)=E[e^{tX}] for t in an open interval around 0; write Σe^{tx}p(x) or ∫e^{tx}f(x)dx. Expand M_X(t)=1+μ′₁t+μ′₂t²/2!+…; hence μ′ᵣ=M_X^{(r)}(0). State M_X(0)=1. State uniqueness: if the MGF exists in a neighbourhood of 0, it identifies the distribution. Give linear transform M_{aX+b}(t)=e^{bt}M_X(at). Give sum of independent variables M_{X+Y}(t)=M_X(t)M_Y(t). Mention characteristic function φ(t)=E[e^{itX}] in one line because it always exists; only a few universities compute it here. Use known MGFs only after Unit 3.

figure.aria: Plot of M(t)=1/2+(1/3)e^t+(1/6)e^{2t} over t from −1 to 1; the slope at 0 is 2/3 and the second derivative at 0 is 1.
figure.caption: The curve passes through 1 at t=0; its slope there is E[X]=2/3 and its second derivative gives E[X²]=1.

chapters.trap: Set t=0 after differentiating, not before; MGF may not exist for heavy-tailed variables; M(0)=1 is a quick check.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.5 expectation and moments; exponential series.
chapters.leave: Standard MGFs for binomial, Poisson and normal to Unit 3; characteristic function computations to advanced courses.

chapters.idea: Chebyshev's inequality bounds how much probability can lie far from the mean using only the mean and variance.
chapters.depth: State Markov inequality P(X≥a)≤E[X]/a for X≥0 and a>0. State Chebyshev P(|X−μ|≥kσ)≤1/k² and equivalent P(|X−μ|<kσ)≥1−1/k² for k>1. Prove Chebyshev by applying Markov to (X−μ)². Show that the bound is distribution-free and often loose. Some syllabi call Markov and Chebyshev moment inequalities. Mention use in the weak law of large numbers only as a forward pointer to Unit 4. Do not compute exact probabilities from a named distribution.

figure.aria: Plot of the Chebyshev lower bound 1 − 1/k² for k from 1.1 to 4; at k=2 the bound is 0.75.
figure.caption: The curve is the guaranteed probability inside k standard deviations; at k=2 it reaches 0.75.

chapters.example: A random variable has mean 60 and standard deviation 8. Use Chebyshev to bound P(|X−60|≥16) and P(48<X<72). For |X−60|≥16, k=16/8=2, so the probability is at most 1/4. For 48<X<72, the deviation is below 12, so k=12/8=1.5 and P≥1−1/1.5²=1−4/9=5/9≈0.556.
chapters.trap: The inequality gives bounds, not exact values; k must be greater than 1; Markov needs nonnegative X; check strict versus non-strict intervals.
chapters.leave: Exact tail probabilities to Unit 3 distributions; law of large numbers and central limit theorem to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A function Y=g(X) creates a new random variable whose distribution is inherited from X, with support and multiplicity handled carefully.
chapters.depth: For discrete X, p_Y(y)=Σ_{x:g(x)=y}p_X(x). For continuous X, use the CDF method F_Y(y)=P(g(X)≤y). For a monotone transformation, use f_Y(y)=f_X(g⁻¹(y))|d/dy g⁻¹(y)|. For non-monotone transformations, split the support into branches and add contributions. Cover linear Y=aX+b and simple nonlinear cases such as Y=X² and Y=√X. State the support of Y every time. Some syllabi call this transformation of variables. Joint transformations and Jacobians for two variables are Unit 4.

figure.aria: Plot of the uniform density f_X(x)=1 and the derived density f_Y(y)=1/(2√y) for Y=X²; both have area 1.
figure.caption: For X uniform on (0,1), Y=X² has density 1/(2√y), which is large near 0 but still integrates to 1.

chapters.example: X is uniform on (0,1), so f_X(x)=1 for 0<x<1. Let Y=X². Find the pdf of Y and P(Y≤1/4). The support is 0<y<1. Using x=√y and dx/dy=1/(2√y), f_Y(y)=1/(2√y). P(Y≤1/4)=P(X≤1/2)=1/2.
chapters.trap: Omitting the absolute derivative; forgetting a second preimage in non-monotone maps; giving a formula outside its support; treating y=g(x) as one-to-one when it is not.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.4 pdf/CDF and Chapter 2.5 expectation for checking.
chapters.leave: Joint transformations, Jacobian matrices and derived joint distributions to Unit 4; named distribution results to Unit 3.
